strengths: The paper proposes a simple, potentially useful design point: per-head token selection is recomputed across layers, while scattering outputs back to the full sequence lets previously skipped tokens remain available through the residual stream. This directly addresses a limitation of permanent token-eviction methods.

The evaluation covers two long-context model families and multiple benchmarks, including RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack. Results consistently show small accuracy changes when the method is added to FlashAttention, MInference, or FlexPrefill.

The compositional results are promising. For example, on LLaMA-3.1-8B at 128K, adding the method increases the reported attention speedup from 2.44x to 2.76x for FlexPrefill while leaving average RULER accuracy unchanged at 87.27%.
The paper includes relevant ablations: dynamic versus fixed sparsity, coverage sweeps, latency-overhead decomposition, layer-drift analysis, and matched-speed comparisons with FastKV and GemFilter.

The presentation is generally clear and the main mechanism is easy to understand. The limitations section honestly acknowledges reduced short-context gains and accuracy risks from aggressive sparsification; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The principal efficiency claim is supported only by attention latency averaged across layers, not end-to-end prefill latency, time-to-first-token, peak memory, or serving throughput. Gather/scatter, scoring, indexing, QKV projection, MLP, communication, and framework overhead can substantially dilute attention-only gains, so the evidence does not yet establish practical inference acceleration.

Important methodological details needed to establish soundness are missing. The recent-query count in Algorithm 1 is unspecified; it is unclear whether selected indices are restored to original positional order before causal FlashAttention; and the treatment of grouped-query attention in both evaluated models is not explained. Per-query-head K/V selection may require replicating shared KV heads and materially alter costs.

Selection for every query position is derived from the most recent queries. Thus the computation performed for an earlier token can depend on later prompt tokens, even though its retained attention remains causally masked. The paper neither discusses this loss of prefix consistency nor analyzes its consequences for causal semantics, prompt caching, chunked prefill, or reuse of prefix KV states.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no code or artifact, and the manuscript omits batch size, dtype, FlashAttention/Triton versions, compilation settings, timing protocol, warmups and repetitions, variance, exact generation/evaluation settings, recent-query count, and baseline implementation details. The drift-preprocessing data are also unspecified.

The layer-selection procedure is insufficiently validated. Representation drift is correlated with RULER accuracy on the same 4K benchmark used in evaluation, but there is no held-out calibration protocol, comparison against stronger layer-selection heuristics, or ablation separating the effects of interleaving, per-head selection, and drift-based layer selection.

The empirical scope is narrower than the claims suggest: only two related decoder-only models and one A100 GPU are tested, with no batch-size scaling, newer hardware, longer-context model families, chunked prefill, or system-level serving evaluation. Several benchmark differences are small enough that uncertainty matters, but no confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics are reported.

The novelty is meaningful but incremental: gather-selected Q/K/V, run standard attention, scatter back, and rely on residual preservation is a straightforward combination of token pruning and sparse attention. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this mechanism from prior token-selective propagation beyond the reversibility and per-head-selection framing.

Some claims overreach the evidence. The assertion that the method removes only irrelevant tokens is not established, and the advertised 3.23x result uses a more aggressive coverage setting than the main configuration. The appendix also mislabels Figure 7 as a latency breakdown although it contains Needle-in-a-Haystack heatmaps. Overall, the idea is promising, but missing causal/system details and incomplete reproducibility prevent reliable acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The compress-attend-scatter design is simple and potentially useful: it preserves the full residual-stream sequence between layers, permits layer- and head-dependent reselection, and can reuse optimized dense attention kernels. This is a meaningful systems design point between permanent token eviction and block-sparse attention.

The evaluation covers two public long-context models and several benchmarks, including RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack. The consistent, relatively small accuracy changes suggest that moderate sparsification can preserve behavior in the tested settings.

The reported attention-level improvements are credible and practically relevant within their stated scope. For example, on LLaMA-3.1-8B at 128K, Token Sparse raises FlashAttention speed from 1.00x to 1.36x and FlexPrefill from 2.44x to 2.76x while approximately preserving average RULER accuracy.

The paper includes useful comparisons with fixed sparsity and token-eviction baselines, an overhead breakdown, and measurements across context lengths. It also honestly notes reduced benefits at short contexts and the risk of removing important tokens under aggressive sparsification.

The manuscript is generally readable, and the main compression/decompression mechanism is easy to understand from Figure 3. The work raises no material research-ethics concerns: it uses public models and benchmarks, involves no human-subject study, and introduces no evident application-specific harm. weaknesses: Soundness: the evidence does not isolate the paper's central claimed advantages. There is no controlled ablation of reversible interleaving versus permanent eviction, per-head versus shared-head selection, dynamic layer selection versus a fixed layer set, or recent-query scoring alternatives. Table 5 compares complete methods and therefore cannot establish that reversibility or head-specific selection causes the observed advantage.

The sparse-layer rule is weakly validated and then extrapolated substantially. Its supporting experiment uses random three-layer subsets on only LLaMA-3.1-8B and 4K RULER, whereas the final method sparsifies half the layers and is evaluated on another model and contexts up to 256K. Representation drift is shown to correlate with accuracy, but no comparison against simpler layer-selection heuristics or held-out calibration establishes that it is necessary or generalizes.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The crucial number of recent queries, pooling operation, calibration data used to estimate representation drift, selected layer indices, handling of grouped-query attention, Triton implementation, software versions, batching, warm-up and repetition protocol, and detailed FastKV/GemFilter settings are absent. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

The practical-efficiency claims exceed the measurements. Reported speedups concern average attention latency rather than end-to-end prefill or request latency, and all experiments use one A100. Gather/scatter, QKV projection, MLP, memory consumption, and framework overhead can materially reduce application-level gains. Throughput, peak memory, and multi-GPU behavior are not reported.

The strongest speedups are easy to misinterpret: the roughly 3.23x result is obtained by composing the method with an already-fast FlexPrefill baseline and is expressed relative to FlashAttention. The incremental improvement over FlexPrefill at the principal setting is much smaller, from 2.44x to 2.76x. This limits the standalone significance of the contribution.

Evaluation breadth is less convincing than the number of tables suggests. Only two related decoder models and one GPU are tested; no statistical uncertainty or repeated timing variability is reported; several InfiniteBench scores are already near zero; and the 256K efficiency experiment lacks corresponding task-accuracy evidence. It is also unclear whether coverage parameters and sparse layers were selected using the reported evaluation sets, leaving possible tuning leakage.

Originality is moderate. Recomputing token importance and bypassing attention updates for selected token positions is a sensible combination of known token selection, residual preservation, and sparse attention ideas, but the paper provides neither a theoretical result nor sufficiently diagnostic experiments to establish a deeper new principle.

Presentation has several correctness and clarity problems: Algorithm 1 leaves key operations undefined; the symbol L is reused for sequence length and apparently layer count in Equation 2; the meaning of coverage threshold is counterintuitive; and Figure 7's caption incorrectly describes an attention-latency breakdown although the figure presents Needle-in-a-Haystack heatmaps. The limitations section is honest but omits the narrow hardware/model coverage, lack of end-to-end evaluation, calibration dependence, and missing reproducibility details. Overall, the idea has merit, but these evidential and reproducibility gaps outweigh it in the current version.

strengths: Originality/significance: The reversible compress-attend-decompress design is a useful contribution. It permits layer- and head-specific token reselection and composes naturally with FlashAttention, Minference, and FlexPrefill instead of competing with them.

Soundness: Results cover two model families and several long-context benchmarks. RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack generally show small accuracy changes, while matched-speed comparisons against FastKV/GemFilter and dynamic-versus-fixed sparsity ablations support the main design choices.

The efficiency evidence includes scaling with context length, achieved sparsity, and an overhead breakdown. At 128K, adding the method improves reported attention speedups from 1.00x to 1.36x with FlashAttention and from 2.44x to 2.76x with FlexPrefill on LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Presentation: The motivation, algorithm, and experimental narrative are clear, and the figures and tables make the accuracy-efficiency trade-off easy to understand.
Reproducibility is partially supported by named public checkpoints, stated coverage and layer-selection parameters, baseline settings, and the A100 hardware configuration.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges weaker short-context gains, possible accuracy loss under aggressive sparsification, and the restriction to prefill. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for this systems-oriented work. weaknesses: The efficiency claims are based on attention-kernel latency averaged across layers, not end-to-end prefill latency, time to first token, peak memory, or complete generation latency. Consequently, the practical application-level gain may be substantially smaller than the headline attention speedups, especially because default Token Sparse Attention alone reaches only 1.22x–1.36x at 128K.

Important implementation details needed for reproduction are missing: the value of “last q,” the precise pooling operation, whether TopK indices are restored to original positional order before causal attention, Triton kernel details, and the data/sample procedure used to estimate representation drift. Index ordering is particularly important because applying an ordinary causal kernel to importance-ordered tokens could change the causal mask.

The custom implementation is central to the latency result, but no code or kernel artifact is provided in the manuscript. Public checkpoints alone are insufficient to reproduce the claimed system performance.

The evidence for representation drift as the layer-selection criterion is limited to a qualitative plot from 200 random three-layer selections at 4K. No correlation coefficient, uncertainty, comparison against simpler layer heuristics, or demonstration that the calibration generalizes robustly to 128K and unseen task distributions is reported.

All timing experiments use one A100 and only two medium-sized models. There is no evaluation on newer hardware, larger models, batch sizes greater than one, or different kernel stacks, which limits the generality of the systems conclusions.

Reported benchmark values appear to be single runs without uncertainty or significance analysis. Several claimed improvements are only a few tenths of a point and may reflect evaluation noise; the InfiniteBench and LongBench averages often decrease slightly.

The limitations discussion does not address the absence of end-to-end measurements, dependence on offline layer calibration, hardware portability, or the incomplete implementation specification. Overall, the idea is useful and the empirical results are encouraging, but these limitations make this a weak rather than clear accept.

strengths: Soundness: The compress-attend-scatter design is plausible and supported by unusually broad evidence: RULER and InfiniteBench results on two model families, additional LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack experiments, comparisons with eviction and non-eviction methods, and ablations of scoring, dynamic budgets, and layer selection. Tables 1–2 show that the default setting generally preserves baseline accuracy.

Significance: The method delivers meaningful practical gains in its intended long-context regime. At 128K, Table 10 reports A100 prefill speedups of 1.27× over FlashAttention and 1.85× versus 1.68× for FlexPrefill, while Table 11 shows analogous gains on an A6000. Composition with several sparse-attention methods supports the claimed complementarity.

Originality: Restoring the full sequence after per-head QKV token selection is a simple but useful design point between permanent token eviction and attention-map sparsification. Per-head selection, layer-wise reselection, and drift-based sparse-layer choice form a coherent contribution.
Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, and the main mechanism, motivation, and accuracy–efficiency trade-off are communicated clearly through Figures 2–6 and the accompanying ablations.

The limitations section honestly notes weaker short-context gains, degradation under aggressive sparsification, and the restriction to prefill. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; reducing inference computation could also reduce resource use.
weaknesses: Soundness: The causal-attention implementation is underspecified. Algorithm 1 returns per-head TopK index sets but never states that indices are restored to original sequence order or explains how the original causal mask and positional relationships are preserved after gathering. Applying an ordinary causal FlashAttention kernel to importance-ordered tokens would produce incorrect masking. Moreover, the common subset for all queries is chosen using recent end-of-sequence queries, so earlier-token computation is conditioned on later prompt content through the selection pattern. The paper should precisely characterize this departure from ordinary causal prefill and ablate whether it affects results or KV-cache behavior.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for a systems contribution. There is no code or kernel release, and essential details are absent: the value of `last_q`, the exact pooling operation, tie handling and ordering after TopK, treatment of GQA heads and mandatory/special tokens, precision and software versions, batch size, warm-up and timing protocol, number of latency repetitions, and the data used to estimate representation drift. These omissions make both correctness and reported speedups difficult to verify.

There is a consequential parameter inconsistency: Section 2.4 describes token coverage as 0.99, whereas Algorithm 1 defines τ as the cumulative mass of discarded low-score tokens and the main experiments use τ=0.005 or 0.008. The manuscript must reconcile retained coverage, discarded mass, and attention-map sparsity. Other notation is also ambiguous, including reuse of L for sequence length and number of layers in Eq. 2.

The strongest headline speedups are attention-kernel rather than end-to-end gains. The practical A100 gain over dense attention is 1.27× at 128K, not the abstract's 3.23×, and the method slightly slows dense prefill at 8K (0.97× on A100 and 0.86× on A6000). Reporting only 8K and 128K end-to-end latency leaves the crossover point and operational range unclear; memory use and peak workspace are also omitted despite per-head gather/scatter buffers.

The evidence for drift-based layer selection risks calibration dependence. Figure 4 and Tables 8–9 show correlation and a useful ranking, but the paper does not specify the calibration corpus, sample count, transfer to unseen domains, or comparison against simpler fixed layer schedules. The choice δ=0.5 and the primary τ values appear tuned on RULER without a clean held-out selection protocol.

Evaluation changes are mostly sub-percentage-point but no uncertainty is reported for task accuracy, while some individual InfiniteBench and LongBench tasks decline noticeably. Results cover only two medium-sized model families and primarily one GPU generation, limiting claims of generality. The limitations discussion does not acknowledge these reproducibility, calibration, causal-semantics, memory, or model-coverage limitations. Overall, the idea and empirical scope are promising, but these unresolved correctness and reproducibility questions outweigh the merits in the current version.

strengths: Originality: Interleaving per-head Q/K/V token selection with scattering back to the full sequence is a sensible, lightweight design that distinguishes the method from irreversible token eviction. The manuscript also explores the useful design point of composing token sparsity with block-sparse attention. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/8456b48a754d4485846366343e4d2aa2/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Soundness: The experiments cover RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, multiple sparsity levels, fixed-versus-dynamic budgets, layer-selection ablations, and several dense, sparse, eviction, and non-eviction baselines.

Significance: The method produces measurable long-context prefill gains. At 128K on A100, adding it to FlashAttention reduces reported prefill latency from 31.04 s to 24.35 s, while adding it to FlexPrefill reduces latency from 18.45 s to 16.81 s.
Presentation: The central compress-attend-scatter mechanism is intuitive and generally well illustrated. Tables expose both accuracy and efficiency rather than reporting sparsity alone.

Limitations and ethics: The paper acknowledges reduced benefit at short contexts, degradation under aggressive sparsification, and its restriction to prefill. The work presents low direct ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: Essential parts of the algorithm are underspecified. The number of recent queries denoted by "last q" is never given, the pooling operation in Algorithm 1 is undefined, and it is unclear whether special or recent tokens are forcibly retained. These choices directly determine both accuracy and overhead.

Soundness: The drift-based layer selection is weakly validated and potentially circular. Drift is computed from the entire transformer-layer update, including the MLP, although only attention is sparsified. The paper selects and validates layers using RULER results, but does not identify an independent calibration set, report a correlation coefficient, or demonstrate transfer of a layer set selected without access to evaluation tasks. The claimed model-agnostic reliability is therefore unsupported.

Soundness: Baseline comparisons do not consistently match the actual resources saved. Table 5 matches token-eviction methods by attention speedup even though those methods may also skip downstream token or FFN computation; the appendix itself recognizes this issue and switches to prefill speedup for OrthoRank. Consequently, the headline advantage over eviction methods is not established on a fair end-to-end basis.

Soundness: The claimed compatibility with standard attention kernels needs substantially more technical evidence. Both evaluated models use grouped-query attention, yet the paper does not explain how independently selected query-head token sets interact with shared K/V heads, whether K/V tensors are replicated, or how that affects memory traffic and latency. Likewise, applying positional block-sparse patterns after arbitrary token gathering changes their meaning in original-sequence coordinates.

Evidence and significance: The headline speedups are attention-kernel figures and partly inherit large gains from the underlying sparse baseline. End-to-end prefill gains are much smaller—for example, 1.27x for Token Sparse over FlashAttention and only about 1.10x incremental improvement over FlexPrefill on A100 at 128K. At 8K, the method slightly slows FlashAttention. The abstract and main discussion do not adequately distinguish these quantities.

Evidence: Evaluation is limited to two 8B–12B models with similar decoder architectures and one primary hardware generation. Mistral-Nemo is already near floor on several long-context tasks (including 0 on Retr.KV and 19.68 RULER at 128K), so preserving those scores provides weak evidence that important information is retained. There are no larger models, alternative architectural families, controlled worst-case retrieval tests, or output-quality analyses beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

Evidence: Many reported differences are only a few tenths of a point, but accuracy tables provide no uncertainty, number of examples, repeated-run analysis, or statistical tests. Figure 4(b) summarizes 200 trials only visually, without quantitative correlation or uncertainty. Claims such as "consistently" preserving accuracy and removing "only irrelevant tokens" are stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility: No code or artifact availability statement is provided. The manuscript omits the exact recent-query count, pooling definition, calibration prompts and sample counts for drift, benchmark configurations, generation settings, warm-up and timing protocol, kernel details, and many baseline hyperparameters. Reconstructing either the method or its latency results would require substantial guesswork.

Presentation: Terminology is confusing: τ is called token coverage, but Algorithm 1 uses it as cumulative attention mass to remove, so increasing "coverage" increases pruning. The algorithm also chooses the minimum prefix whose removed mass exceeds τ, rather than clearly enforcing a maximum discarded-mass constraint. This overshoot is not discussed.

Originality: The scatter-to-residual construction is a modest variation on selective token propagation/non-eviction mechanisms. The closest non-eviction comparison, OrthoRank, appears only in the appendix, and the related-work discussion does not sharply establish which parts beyond per-head selection and the scoring heuristic are technically new.

Limitations and ethics: The generic impact statement is acceptable for a low-risk efficiency paper, but the limitations discussion is incomplete. It does not address calibration-data dependence, adversarial or distributed evidence that recent-query scoring may miss, task-dependent failures, GQA implementation costs, benchmark contamination, or the mismatch between attention-level and end-to-end gains.

Overall: The idea is promising and the empirical package is sizable, but unresolved specification, fairness, calibration, and reproducibility problems prevent confidence in the central generality and efficiency claims. Substantial revision is needed before others could reliably reproduce or build on the contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful idea: compressing Q/K/V to independently selected per-head token subsets, then scattering attention outputs back to the original sequence, permits tokens to be reconsidered in later layers instead of permanently evicting them. This is a meaningful conceptual distinction from token-eviction methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad across RULER, InfiniteBench, LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, the standalone method improves 128K attention speed by 1.36x while essentially preserving average RULER accuracy (87.01 to 87.02), and it gives complementary gains with several structured-sparse methods.

The paper reports practical end-to-end prefill latency, not only theoretical sparsity or isolated kernel measurements. At 128K, standalone prefill improves from 31.04 to 24.35 seconds on A100 and from 67.34 to 54.49 seconds on A6000; composition with FlexPrefill improves the A100 speedup from 1.68x to 1.85x.

Relevant ablations support several design choices: dynamic budgets outperform approximately speed-matched fixed sparsity, recent-query scoring outperforms random-query and query-pooling alternatives, and low-drift layers are substantially more robust to sparsification than high-drift layers.

The method is training-free and designed to reuse optimized dense or sparse attention kernels. Composition results with FlashAttention, MInference, FlexPrefill, SeerAttention, and X-Attention make the claimed complementarity reasonably convincing.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. Its limitations section appropriately acknowledges weaker short-context gains and the accuracy risk from aggressive sparsification. The work raises no unresolved material ethical concern and may reduce inference compute.
weaknesses: Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing. In particular, the number of recent queries (“last q”), pooling operation, causal masking details, handling of positional encodings, preprocessing data used to estimate layer drift, kernel configuration, and timing protocol or number of repetitions are not fully specified. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

The models evaluated use grouped-query attention, yet the paper describes independently gathering Q, K, and V for every attention head without explaining how distinct query-head selections interact with shared KV heads. Duplicating K/V per query head could materially affect memory, latency, and kernel compatibility, so this omission leaves an important part of the implementation and efficiency claim unclear.

The soundness evidence is empirical rather than theoretical, and some descriptions overstate the mechanism. Scattering zeros at unselected query positions bypasses the attention sublayer for those positions; it is not simply equivalent to masking individual entries of an ordinary attention map, nor does retaining tokens through the residual preserve the full expressive flexibility of dense attention within that layer.

Generality is limited by evaluation on only two moderately sized, closely related decoder models. Results on larger models, other architectural families, multimodal settings, batch sizes above one, and production serving workloads are absent. The claim of broad compatibility would be stronger with these tests and memory-usage measurements.

Accuracy results are mostly single point estimates without uncertainty or significance analysis. Several reported differences are small enough to be evaluation noise, while some InfiniteBench compositions show nontrivial degradation—for example, FlexPrefill plus the method falls from 49.53 to 49.23 on LLaMA and from 24.80 to 24.08 on Mistral.

The drift-based layer selection is a model-specific preprocessing heuristic whose cost, calibration dataset, and stability across domains are insufficiently characterized. Figure 4 uses a 4K RULER experiment to motivate selection later applied through 128K, creating some risk of benchmark- or configuration-specific tuning.

The practical benefit is concentrated at very long contexts: at 8K, standalone Token Sparse Attention is slightly slower than FlashAttention on both A100 and A6000. Decoding remains dense with the full KV cache, so the method does not address memory capacity or per-token decoding cost, which are also major long-context deployment bottlenecks.
